p.src: Two Frames on One Railroad Track

u.src: Two Frames on One Railroad Track
en: Two Frames on One Railroad Track

p.src: The Lorentz transformation derived previously concerned a deliberately restricted geometry: every relative motion lay along one axis. Picture a long railroad track. One set of observers remains at the station; another set rides in a train moving along the track. The transverse directions are present, but they play no role until they are restored later.

p.src: Each frame is an operational coordinate system. Meter sticks at rest in the frame define spatial coordinates, and synchronized clocks at rest in the frame define time. The postulate that fixes their relationship is that every inertial observer measures the same speed of light.

p.src: Most calculations will use $c=1$. Time may be measured in seconds and distance in light-seconds, or in years and light-years. Velocities then become dimensionless fractions of light speed. When ordinary units are needed, factors of $c$ are restored uniquely by dimensional consistency; for example, $v^2$ in a dimensionless Lorentz factor becomes $v^2/c^2$.

p.src: Direct and inverse transformations

u.src: Direct and inverse transformations
en: Direct and inverse transformations

p.src:
Let a flash occur somewhere in or near the train. It is one event, independent of who describes it. The station observer assigns $(x,t)$, while the train observer assigns $(x',t')$. In units $c=1$, $\begin{aligned}
x'&=\gamma_v(x-vt),&
t'&=\gamma_v(t-vx),
\\
\gamma_v&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}.\end{aligned}$ Newton would recognize the displacement $x-vt$; the factor $\gamma_v$ and the mixing of $x$ into $t'$ are the relativistic changes.

p.src:
Reciprocity gives the inverse by reversing the sign of the relative velocity: $\begin{aligned}
x&=\gamma_v(x'+vt'),&
t&=\gamma_v(t'+vx').
\end{aligned}$ The station is not absolutely at rest. It is merely the frame called unprimed, and the train sees it moving at $-v$.

p.src: Three Frames and the Composition of Boosts

u.src: Three Frames and the Composition of Boosts
en: Three Frames and the Composition of Boosts

p.src: Place a small kiddie car inside the train. The train moves at speed $v$ relative to the station, while the car moves down the aisle at speed $u$ relative to the train passenger. Call the speed of the car relative to the station $w$. Newtonian intuition suggests $w=u+v$, but the Lorentz transformations must decide.

Call the speed of the car relative to the station $w$. Newtonian intuition suggests $w=u+v$, but the Lorentz transformations must decide.

p.src:
There are now three coordinate systems: $(x,t),\qquad (x',t'),\qquad (x'',t'').$ The first belongs to the station, the second to the train, and the third to the car. Between the train and the car, $\begin{aligned}
x''&=\gamma_u(x'-ut'),&
t''&=\gamma_u(t'-ux'),
\\
\gamma_u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}.\end{aligned}$

There are now three coordinate systems: $(x,t),\qquad (x',t'),\qquad (x'',t'').$ The first belongs to the station, the second to the train, and the third to the car. Between the train and the car, $\begin{aligned}
x''&=\gamma_u(x'-ut'),&
t''&=\gamma_u(t'-ux'),
\\
\gamma_u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}.\end{aligned}$

p.src: Substitute one boost into the other

u.src: Substitute one boost into the other
en: Substitute one boost into the other

p.src:
The spatial equation is enough to find $w$. Substitute  into the first equation of : $\begin{aligned}
x''
&=\gamma_u(x'-ut')\\
&=\gamma_u\gamma_v\left[(x-vt)-u(t-vx)\right]\\
&=\gamma_u\gamma_v\left[(1+uv)x-(u+v)t\right].
\end{aligned}$ The two minus signs in the $uvx$ term make it positive; the two time terms combine as $-(u+v)t$.

p.src: As before, the denominator is irrelevant when locating the moving origin. The kiddie car is at rest at $x''=0$, so the bracket in  must vanish: $(1+uv)x-(u+v)t=0.$ Its station-frame worldline is therefore $x=\frac{u+v}{1+uv}\,t,$ and its velocity is $\boxed{w=\frac{u+v}{1+uv}}.$

The transformation laws themselves are universal and independent of the train’s walls.

p.src: The Proper Interval in Three Spatial Dimensions

u.src: The Proper Interval in Three Spatial Dimensions
en: The Proper Interval in Three Spatial Dimensions

p.src:
Return to two events, initially one at the origin and the other at $(x,t)$. In one spatial dimension, $\tau^2=t^2-x^2$ in units $c=1$. Every inertial frame agrees: $\tau^2
=t^2-x^2
=t'^2-x'^2
=t''^2-x''^2.$ The coordinates change; the proper interval does not.

u.src: Null Rays and the Light Cone
en: Null Rays and the Light Cone

p.src: In one space dimension, right- and left-moving light rays satisfy $x=\pm t.$ Their interval vanishes: $t^2-x^2=0.$ Unlike Euclidean distance, a zero spacetime interval does not require coincident events. It means that a light signal can connect them.

p.src: From Spatial Vectors to Four-Vectors

u.src: From Spatial Vectors to Four-Vectors
en: From Spatial Vectors to Four-Vectors

p.src:
The vectors here are geometric vectors, not quantum state vectors. A displacement between two points in ordinary space has magnitude and direction. Its tail can be translated to the origin without changing the vector, and its three components may be denoted $x^i=(x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x,y,z),
\qquad i=1,2,3.$ The Latin index $i$ runs only over spatial directions.

\qquad i=1,2,3.$ The Latin index $i$ runs only over spatial directions.

\qquad i=1,2,3.$ The Latin index $i$ runs only over spatial directions.

p.src:
An event needs one additional component, its time. A spacetime position is therefore written $x^\mu=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(t,x,y,z),
\qquad \mu=0,1,2,3.$ By historical convention time is the zeroth component rather than the fourth: $x^0=t,\qquad x^1=x,\qquad x^2=y,\qquad x^3=z.$ Greek indices such as $\mu$ run over spacetime; Latin indices such as $i$ run over space.

Move from the position of one event to a short segment of a particle’s worldline. The four-displacement is $\Delta x^\mu
=(\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z).$ When a displacement is called small, calculus is approaching: $\Delta x^\mu$ will become $dx^\mu$. For the moment, the finite notation makes the geometry transparent.

p.src: This object has four components and transforms as a four-vector. Its relation to ordinary three-velocity is the next question, deliberately left open here. Resolving it leads toward relativistic momentum, energy, acceleration, and ultimately the relativistic generalization of $F=ma$.
